sets.p:
Dear All,
I would like to adress the incidents which have occured during the past month in the office kitchen as these have escalated from a minor irritation to a repeated, deliberite and obtuse disregard for the office etiquette, which we all agreed upon adhering to one we joined the company and took up our positions, voluntarily, at this location rather than another office within this country, but, I will not let this stop me from making my point, which is, in short, PLEASE ensure that you do not consume the blue-topped organic almond milk in the fridge, which is easily identifable as Roger’s property due to it being labelled with a sticky note with the name, ‘Roger,’ written in black marker pen. Warnings and sanctions will be issued as soon as the perpetrator is found. Seniour management will be notified. Roger
i: “I would like to adress”
address
‘Address’ is spelt with two of the letters ‘d’ and ‘s.’ In this sense, ‘address’ means to bring something into focus or to be made aware of something.
“…which have occured during…”
occurred
‘Occurred’ is spelt with two of the letters ‘c’ and ‘r’. Misspellings are typically made by forgetting to include both of the c’s and r’s.
“…irritation to a repeated, deliberite and obtuse disregard…”
deliberate
‘Deliberate’ is spelt with an ‘a’ not an ‘i’. This is quite a common misspelling.
“…adhering to one we joined…”
once

This misspelling has altered the meaning of the sentence such that it does not make sense. ‘Once’ fits better within the context of the sentence, to indicate that after an event had occurred it meant that another was taking place.
“…which is easily identifable as…”
identifiable

There is a slightly difficult to spot misspelling with the word ‘identifable.’ Unfortunately, ‘identifable’ does not mean anything as it is not a word. From a simple guess with what’s already presented within the rest of the clause, it can be quite easy to see that the word should be ‘identifiable’ and all that was missing from it was an ‘i’ before the last ‘a’.
“Seniour management will be notified.”
Senior
‘Senior’ is spelt without the ‘u.’ The spelling of ‘Senior’ with a ‘u’ is now obsolete.

sets.g: Passage A is more casual and expressive in its language than passage B. Some might say that identifying Roger by name removes a level of anonymity and professionality. The use of part of the idiom ‘crying…over spilt milk’ is mocking in tone. Passage B has an air of secrecy, which might be interpreted as formal, but could more accurately be described as evasive or elusive; it’s quite vague in the events and it’s describing, perhaps only those in the know would have a better idea of the e-‘mail’ and ‘involvement’ being discussed here.
sets.p:
A. Have you seen the e-mail Roger’s sent out to the entire office?! I can’t believe he’s thinking of crying to senior management over spilt milk!
B. You must’ve read the e-mail which was sent out recently. We may need to keep our involvement in this quiet in case the situation escalates.
i: It’s hilarious! “Spilt milk;” quite literally. I’d have no idea he’d take it this far. Do you reckon he knows we did it?
A
The use of punctuation here presents the language to be quite expressive in a similar style to passage A, rather than reserved, which is passage B.
We might have gone too far there, although it was only a joke, I think we should, you know, talk to him and resolve this. We’ll just tell him it was silly.
A

The language in this passage is apologetic and sympathetic in tone, almost guilty, which is quite unlike the tone of passage A. Still, it is the style of language which must be considered, and, as identified in the previous response, the language used is quite informal, which fits the style of passage A better than passage B.
I’m absolutely aware of the situation I believe you’re referring to. It will not be as grave as you think as I’ve already put plans in place to limit our liability should the threats be carried out.
B
The language used here is a more appropriate response to Passage B, due to the secrecy, vagueness and hint of professionalism underwritten within the formal vocabulary.
As we’ve been working diligently on this project I’m certain that our achievements will overshadow any discrepancies which may have happened because of our actions.
B

The language is formal and clinical; all emotion has been removed, including anything which could leave the person writing this culpable of certain actions. The absence of emotive language is far closer to passage B in style, than A.
Yes, I have! This will be such a massive pain should it get out of hand like it did with Sophie last year.
A

This response is similar in the language style to passage A because it mentions another person by name and relates them to a similar incident. The terms ‘get out of hand’ is not to be taken literally, just like ‘crying…over spilt milk’ is an idiom used in passage A. The use of the term ‘a massive pain’ is not to be taken literally, and might be seen as an exaggeration of the actual gravity of the issue being discussed. Lastly, the use of punctuation gives off the impression with this response that the recipient is shocked and has something to be exclamatory over. This is very similar to passage A, more so than passage B which does not use punctuation in this manner. Passage B keeps the tone rather bland, placid or reserved with the use of its full stops and no other punctuation marks.

sets.p:
This letter was written by an employee higher up in the company’s hierarchy than those mentioned and involved in the previous passages, and she has asked the office undergraduate intern to check it for any spelling mistakes.

An incident has come to my attention. I have spoken with the two employees involved (whom / who), upon being reprimanded, have expressed deep regret at their actions. They have both come to the realisation that the (actions / axioms) they took were (holy/wholly) inappropriate and have shown promise that they will, in the future, adhere to the practices this company seeks to uphold. The self- raising organic (flour/flower) left after the office (baking / backing) competition has been returned to its original owner.
i: “I have spoken with the two employees involved (whom / who)”
whom
who
B

The difference between who and whom is a subtle, yet important, one, similar to ‘him’ and ‘he,’ or ‘I’ and ‘me.’ Remember, whom is used to determine the object of the sentence, whereas who is used to determine the subject. In this case, since the ‘upon being reprimanded’ is parenthetical, it should be ‘who’.
“…that the (actions / axioms) they took…”
actions
axioms
A

Axioms can be considered starting points, taken be true, from which an argument or idea can develop. Actions, however, are the moves made, usually consciously, by people, sometimes when there is a gain, measurable or not, to be made. From the context of the sentence, ‘actions’ make far more sense, and is the correct word to choose from.
“…they took were (holy / wholly) inappropriate”
holy
wholly
B

Two similar sounding words with quite different spellings. Holy is related to religious language, whereas wholly is a word used to define the entirety of a thing. It is synonymous with; fully, and entirely.
“The self-raising organic (flour / flower) left…”
flour
flower
A

These words sound exactly the same in speech, it’s key to pay attention to what else is being said to identify which noun is being talked about. The key words here are ‘self-raising’ and ‘organic.’ Self-raising is the biggest give away that flour, used in cooking, is the correct word here.
“…after the office (backing / baking) competition…”
backing
baking
B

The answer to this question can be determined by the context; an office baking competition seems far more likely to be the case than an office backing competition. Also consider that earlier in the sentence we determined that flour had been used, and flour is used many baking recipes, so this further reinforces evidence that ‘baking’ is the correct word here.

sets.p:
1. You are an absolute disgrace to yourself and to this company. Consider this your third and final reprimand from myself. The remainder of the board have still to reach a decision regarding your employment contract with us.
2. After reviewing the transgressions which have been brought to my attention, I have declared this issue to have been resolved peacefully. I must first thank you for your well-balanced composure during this time.
3. I send my congratulations to the Diversity team; you have done fantastically well at championing for diversity in the workplace through your unusual, yet well-received, recruitment program.
4. I am so, so, so ecstatic to hear that you will be working more closely with us! I offer you my heartfelt congratulations on your successful internal application to the position.
5. We are all fairly pleased for you that you passed the second round of the application process, despite our initial reservations on your public-speaking abilities.
i: You are an absolute disgrace to yourself and to this company. Consider this your third and final reprimand from myself. The remainder of the board have still to reach a decision regarding your employment contract with us.
5th

This response manages to regain some restraint towards after the first sentence. The first sentence uses particularly strong and negative language to express the writer’s feelings, certainly the strongest negative feelings amongst all of the responses here. There is little to suggest, from the rest of the passage, that the writer’s opinion has swayed. Hence, it is ranked the least positive in 5th place.

After reviewing the transgressions which have been brought to my attention, I have declared this issue to have been resolved peacefully. I must first thank you for your well-balanced composure during this time.
3rd

This response maintains a neutral tone throughout. There is no indication of any positivity or negativity, other than a polite, formal thank you offered for, what might be considered, standard behaviour. This statement is ranked 3rd based on its neutrality.
I send my congratulations to the Diversity team; you have done fantastically well at championing for diversity in the workplace through your unusual, yet well-received, recruitment program.
2nd

This response is amongst the only two which express any feeling of positivity. It’s hampered by the slightly sceptical tone revolving around the phrase ‘…your unusual, yet well-received, recruitment program,’ which we could almost interpret that the person stating this was not pleased to have been surprised by the new methods employed. Still, there is an element of a positive tone which ranks it above the first response of explicit disgust.
I am so, so, so ecstatic to hear that you will be working more closely with us! I offer you my heartfelt congratulations on your successful internal application to the position.
1st

This response is, when compared with the others, the most positive. The repetition of ‘so, so, so’ – essentially, in this instance, superlatives – conveys how, perhaps indescribably, pleased the respondent is with the news they’ve received. ‘Ecstatic’ is a far stronger word to describe a positive emotion than ‘well.’
We are all fairly pleased for you that you passed the second round of the application process, despite our initial reservations on your public-speaking abilities.
4th

There are subtle undertones of displeasure within this message to the level which could be described as passive-aggressiveness. This introduction then moves on to the phrase ‘despite my initial reservations on your …abilities,’ which highlights the doubts which were held, which could be seen as a lack of confidence in the person, or perhaps something slightly nastier, jealousy perhaps. The negativity in this statement is only surpassed by number 5 which is outright hostility from the start.

sets.p: Mark and Stuart had been found to have been using some of the food Roger had left in the office fridge without permission from Roger. The item which caused the most upset was the organic almond milk, understandably, because only a drop was left of it and it is necessary for Roger to have with his tea due to his lactose- intolerance. Mark’s defence was to say that he is also lactose-intolerant, but we haven’t received any notes from the doctor just yet. After litigation, Mark, Stuart and Roger have settled the compensation Roger felt was due to him.
i: Mark and Stuart had taken some of Roger’s marmalade without his permission.
Cannot Say

Cannot Say – The passage isn’t specific as to which foodstuffs Mark and Stuart have been ‘borrowing’ from Roger without his permission. Clearly, something was misappropriated, but, as to what, this isn’t made certain.
Very little almond milk remained.
True
True – The passage states in the second sentence that, ‘only a drop was left of [organic almond milk].’
Mark and Stuart have repaid in full Roger for the goods they took.
Cannot Say

Cannot Say – The passages states in the final sentence that the three of them reached a settlement point, whether this is that Mark and Stuart have repaid Roger in full is not known. They might have paid more or less than the cost of the goods they took.
Mark has proven that he is also lactose-intolerant.
False

False – As stated in the second last sentence of the passage Mark attempted to use this in his defence, but he was unable to provide any medical evidence for it. He may be lactose- intolerant, and this is not what is in dispute in the question, but rather whether any evidence has been put forward to support this. So far, nothing. Therefore, the answer is false.
This event will not happen in future.
Cannot Say
Cannot Say – There is no mention of any measures put in place to prevent this from happening again. Therefore, we cannot say.

sets.g: Passage A is very conversational in tone, it is informal language, the thoughts and ideas are not clearly laid out, details are missing. We can imagine a scenario where two people are chatting over the issue. Passage B uses very technical language common within scientific papers. Information is conveyed in a very dense format, without the use of superlatives. Instructions are written in the 3rd person and observations are noted. Although, you may not understand the science between the methods, it is important to note clearly the style shown.
sets.p:
A. “Anyway, Jaz, as I was saying, Kerry couldn’t believe that Jason had called her, “disgusting,” yesterday. But, Sally said that he said that because she said to him the other night that he was boring and was thinking of leaving him. It was only natural for him to flip out.”
B. 0.573g of CuCl2 was dissolved with 10ml of H2O in a conical flask. 2ml of NaOH were added to the solution. The clear blue liquid formed a dark green precipitate. 2ml of HCl were added and the mixture returned to a clear blue solution.
i: The plant was uprooted from the living room and reseated in the garden. It was watered every day for 5 days. After which time it looked healthier and its leaves were no longer wilting. Little buds had appeared on the branches by the 9th day.
B

This passage does not detail an experiment, this could have been anybody’s descriptive recollection of the actions they took to bring their plant to better health. The language is the key determining factor here, a living room is not a laboratory, but it is still a detail which is necessary to perhaps explain anything noted afterwards. The passage employs the 3rd person to describe the plant and does not lapse into the 1st person when detailing events (e.g. I moved the plant outside). The observations after the action was performed are key in mimicking the style of passage B over A.
Of course, I spoke to him earlier on the phone. I expect him to arrive at 5pm. We’ll stay at the house for a while, and when I’m ready we’ll go out for dinner.
A

The response is casual in tone, yet informative. However, it can be clearly seen that the passage is written in the 1st person, which is used heavily in passage A, whereas passage B avoids this at every opportunity. For example, ‘I expect him to arrive at 5pm’ would have to be written as ‘he is expected to arrive at 5pm’ for it to mimic the writing style of passage B.
The Elizabeth line will run from Reading to Shenfield. Each train will be 9 carriages long. The expected journey time from Heathrow Terminal 4 to Paddington Station is 30 minutes.
B

This is a slightly trickier one. The content isn’t what you’d describe as gossip, it is still informative, and there are no references to the 1st person. It is something which you could expect to read in a leaflet, and hence fits the style of passage B.
You should have seen how she reacted when she discovered that she had earned a place on the engineering apprenticeship course starting in September. She was so pleased!
A

Once again, the passage is very informative, and many opportunities are taken to use the 3rd person: ‘she reacted’, ‘she discovered,’ ‘she was so pleased.’ These, excluding the first pronoun, along with the observation made all point towards passage B, but the tone is conversational in the sense that the passage is addressing a person. Passage A is addressing another person, whereas passage B isn’t addressing anyone in particular. The first pronoun along with the lack of brevity to the actions and observations make this passage more in the style of passage A, rather than B.
So, I then added the dowels, I think, to the ends of the planks before slotting them, not so neatly, into the holes of panel A. And now, it looks alright.
A

The content here is instructional and observational, it follows style B strictly in context, and loosely in style. The conversational tone taken up with the use of ‘so’ to begin the passage is very different to style B, where no unnecessary vocabulary is used. The passage does continue in this manner, when it describes an action as ‘not so neatly’ done, which is different to style A’s observations are on the effects which occurred as a result of the actions taken, not as the actions were being taken.

sets.p: As we move ever further forward into this millenium we have no idea how conscience life will shape our planet. It is important for us to maintain piece amongst ourselves for us to better do our peace in supporting, sustaining, preserving and conserving the nature we find all around us. We will be superceded by future generations whom will look back and either thank us for what we’ve saved, or forget us for the damage we’ve reeked upon the planet.
i: “…further forward into this millenium…”
millennium

‘Millenium’ with one ‘n’ is a common misspelling. There are actually two ‘n’s in ‘millennium.’ When practising for this, try to focus on commonly misspelled words, in particular pay close attention to words which have double letters. It is a good practice to write out words which you’ve misspelt, and to return to writing them out repeatedly whenever you make a mistake.
“…we have no idea how conscience life…”
conscious

Within this context ‘conscience’ does not fit. The phrase which might have come to mind whilst reading this section could have been; ‘conscious life,’ often used to refer to humans or other more intelligent animals on the planet. These two words are spelt quite differently, and mean different things. A conscious being can be a person who’s aware of themselves and their existence. A conscience is what dictates a person’s actions based on their judgement of right and wrong.
“…for us to maintain piece amongst ourselves…”
peace

Here is another question where context is crucial, as despite ‘piece’ being spelt correctly, its meaning does not fit with the rest of the sentence. The word here should be ‘peace,’ as this would make more sense to maintain between ourselves, rather than a piece, or slice, of what, exactly?
“…do our peace in supporting…”
piece

Once again, this example is a reversal of the previous one. There is an idiom, ‘do your piece,’ or to say one’s piece means to speak your mind or that one’s individual actions will combine with everybody’s and are, metaphorically, seen as a small chunk when put into an immeasurable perspective amongst everyone’s collective actions.
“We will be superceded by future generations…”
superseded

Another commonly misspelt word; superseded has an ‘s’ where people might expect a ‘c.’ This confusion is exacerbated because it is difficult to know from the soft ‘c’ sound whether it should be spelt with an ‘s’ or ‘c’ if you’re unsure. This is just another word with a spelling which should be committed to memory.
“…damage we’ve reeked upon the planet.”
wrecked

‘Reeked’ would be the past tense conjugation of the verb; to reek, which means for a smell to emanate or permeate from someone or something. The sounds very similar to the verb; wreck, often used when describing destruction or havoc. Although the two words sounds quite similar, and are spelt quite similarly they have different meanings and only one fits the context here.

sets.p:
1. FlowEase will help cut our processing time. Our customers are looking forward to receiving their purchases sooner.
2. The new software implementation sounds quite exciting. Newer members of staff are keen to start their training for the new POS software.
3. Automation will cut journey delays by 90%, but many members of staff are threatening to walk out if the plans go ahead.
4. I’ve heard they’re going to be refurbishing the changing rooms, shall we go and have a look? Lauren says they’re much nicer than before; they’ve even added hairdryers!
5. I’m not sure about these new rules. It is such a simple game, and he’s just trying to make us play Stuck in the mud. I hate that game. I won’t play. You can’t make me.
i: FlowEase will help cut our processing time. Our customers are looking forward to receiving their purchases sooner.
3rd

This seems to be quite a neutral response, there’s no clear excitement or disgust at the change to reduce processing time. In relation to the other responses this ranks 3rd, but the others must be read and determined before this conclusion can be reached.
The new software implementation sounds quite exciting. Newer members of staff are keen to start their training for the new POS software.
2nd
The use of the words ‘keen’ and ‘exciting’ show enthusiasm from the staff and the person speaking.
Automation will cut journey delays by 90%, but many members of staff are threatening to walk out if the plans go ahead.
4th
The response relayed back here is that staff are threatening to take some quite serious industrial action based on the news they’ve heard. But, this is just a threat, no action has yet been taken.
I’ve heard they’re going to be refurbishing the changing rooms, shall we go and have a look? Lauren says they’re much nicer than before; they’ve even added hairdryers!
1st

This response is by far the most positive reception to the changes made, the punctuation accentuates the joy the person is expressing. That they also want to share this with someone else, can be seen as another sign of the warm feeling. Hence why this response is ranked 1st.
I’m not sure about these new rules. It is such a simple game, and he’s just trying to make us play Stuck in the mud. I hate that game. I won’t play. You can’t make me.
5th

The reason why this is considered worse than the threat of strike action is that the individual here, from what has been said, does not want to engage in communication, nor threats, but has gone a step further and taken action to not play the game anymore as he feels that strongly against the new rules implemented. That an action has occurred in this situation, rather than threats, makes it the response least well-received to the news and is ranked 5th.

sets.p: Written with such dedcation to the minutiae of each plot and sub-plot, Bretor Dranoj has delicately interwined the vivid lives of his characters across novels to create a fine mesh of compassion, deciet, suberfuge, and all plays of political power and human vivacity to conjure a world as infinitely varied and entnangled as our own. all future works from this author I’m certain are set to follow the examples already published.
i: “Written with such dedcation…”
dedication
The letter ‘i’ from dedication has been missed out resulting in this simple misspelling.
“…has delicately interwined the vivid…”
intertwined
This is an easy misspelling to gloss over, the second letter ‘t’ from ‘intertwined’ is missing.
“a fine mesh of compassion, deciet…”
deceit
‘Deceit’ is spelt with ‘e’ before ‘i’ (d-e-c-e-i-t); the letters have been transposed in ‘deciet’. The related verb ‘deceive’ follows the same pattern.
“…suberfuge and all plays of political power…”
subterfuge
Another simple misspelling here, there is a letter ‘t’ in ‘subterfuge,’ which has been erroneously omitted.
“…as infinitely varied and entnangled as our own…”
entangled
The misspelling here is with the word ‘entnangled.’ An extra ‘n’ has been added after the first three letters of the word. Removing this letter will correct the spelling of the word.
“all future works…”
All

There isn’t a misspelling in this example, instead punctuation is the issue. Punctuation refers to the rules and conventions, which, when followed, help aid our understanding of the writer’s thoughts. The first letter of a sentence is capitalised, and as there was a full stop after ‘own’ it must follow that the letter ‘a’ in ‘all’ should be capitalised.

sets.p:
A new employee is being given an induction by their new supervisor.

“The office is located on the first floor and the room that’s being leased to us overlooks the park behind. There are half a dozen employees working from this site, and here’s where you will be working starting in, roughly, a weeks’ time. You shall be covering the peak shift; Wednesday to Sunday. We have a seating arrangement and each employee has their own desk, as will you, as soon as yours arrives. We don’t have any spare spaces for the moment. Each desk has a PC, two monitors, a keyboard, mouse, telephone and chair all set up. Cindy’s desk, in the corner, can be raised if you’d prefer to work standing up. She’ll be away on maternity leave for the next few months. You’ll need a key to enter the building at all times and TRENT is the passcode to enter the office during our off-peak hours.”
i: There are currently twice as many monitors as telephones in the office.
True

True – Each desk is stated to have ‘…two monitors…[a] telephone…all set up.’ There are therefore, twice as many monitors as telephones. There is nothing to state otherwise; the new employee’s desk has not yet arrived, and Cindy’s desk doesn’t mention any exceptions to this, just other differences, such as its adjustable height.
A passcode is always required to gain access to the office on weekends.
False

False – Peak shift is described in the third sentence as being from Wednesday to Sunday. This encapsulates the entire weekend; Saturday and Sunday. The passcode is stated, in the last sentence, to be required to enter the office on off-peak hours. As the peak-shift was defined as including Saturday and Sunday, the weekend is therefore part of peak hours, and so no passcode is needed.
The schoolchildren in the park make lots of noise after 3:30pm.
Cannot Say

Cannot Say – There is mention of a park, but there is no mention of schoolchildren creating noise, and although 3:30pm is a standard time for school to finish in the UK, there is no evidence to support this time from the passage either.
The new employee requires a new desk because of their back pain.
Cannot Say
Cannot Say – The new employee does require a new desk. This was mentioned in the fourth sentence of the passage. The reason behind this was explained as each employee having their own desk.
Everyone in the office has a designated place.
True
True – There is a ‘seating arrangement’ in the office, so we can take this to mean that everyone has a place assigned to them. Hence, this statement is true.

sets.g: Passage A represents a formal and considered message. The language is serious and professional. It seems likely to be a message from the museum to a patron rather than from fellow employees. The response to this message must equally be formal and kindly, though perhaps distant and deferential. Passage B represents a less formal message to the receiver. Though serious, it is more familiar and less strict in its use of language. It is perhaps likely that the sender and the receiver are colleagues at the museum or at least know each other at a little bit. As such, the response is perhaps slightly bold, familiar in return.
sets.p:
A. Dear fellow museum patron, it is with great delight to announce that our director will be presenting his latest lecture this month.
B. To whom it may concern, our museum director is going to be lecturing to a limited number this month. If this interests you, let us know.
i: Yes - I am delighted to hear that the dear director shall be lecturing this month!
B

This response is quite casual and very familiar. The overly enthusiastic tone suggests that the sender and receiver perhaps may even know each other at least a little bit, and that they know each other. It could be that they work together at the museum. It is a little bold in statement.
Certainly, I will shall certainly be attending.
A
The language is professional and formal. It seems as if it is from a museum patron fulfilling the request to inform them of their attendance.
Sounds good to me – I’ll be there.
B
The language is quick and casual. As such, this is better suited to the passage B.
Not at all that interested to be honest, I don’t think I’ll make it.
B
There is no sense of deference in the language, nor formal politeness. As such, this is better suited to the passage B.
It is with sincere regret that I will not be able to attend the director’s lecture.
A
The language is formal and reserved, showing deference to the sender. This indicates that this response is better suited to passage A.

sets.p:
Dear Laura,
Our director, I believe you know her well, is due to (make / land / present) a lecture on Parmenides and Pythagoras this month. It should be a wonderful (explaration / exploration / exploretion) into the powerful minds of Ancient Greek philosophy. Unfortunately, we are missing a few vital artefacts that would dramatically help with the visual (accept / aspect / expect) of the presentation. We are, of course, (aware / awared / awares) that they are within your possession. Our director asks whether we could borrow such artefacts from your tore for the following two weeks. You (shall / shallt / shell) be duly compensated. Please let us know your thoughts. Kind regards,
Joanna
i: “…is due to (land / make / present) a lecture on Parmenides and Pythagoras this month.”
Land
Make
Present
C

To ‘land’ a lecture does not make much sense. To ‘make a lecture’ while feasible, does not fit the context of the passage at all. To ‘present’ a lecture is what we want here, describing how the director will undertake or give her lecture.
“It should be a wonderful (explaration / exploration / exploretion) into the powerful minds of Ancient Greek philosophy.”
Explaration
Exploration
Exploretion
B
This is a simple spelling check. The correct spelling is B = ‘exploration’. The others are false.
“…the visual (accept / aspect / expect) of the presentation.”
Accept
Aspect
Expect
B
‘Accept’ the presentation does not work in this context. The ‘visual expect’ is also incorrect. We are looking for the visual ‘aspect’ which denotes the visual part of the presentation.
“We are, of course, (aware / awared / awares) that they are within your possession.”
Aware
Awared
Awares
A
This is a simple grammar check. The correct spelling is A = ‘aware’. The others are false.
“You (shall / shallt / shell) be duly compensated.”
Shall
Shalt
Shell
A
‘Shell’ does not make sense and as a deliberate red herring. ‘Shallt’ is the archaic of Shall, misspelled – thus, also incorrect. The correct answer is ‘shall’.

sets.p:
Dear Joanna,
I would be delighted to offer my support with the director’s lecture on Parmenides and Pythagoras. I presume you were reffering to their respective busts? I have the bust of Parmenides in my collection and I can send that by courrier as soon as possible. The bust of Pythagoras is still on lawn to my dear friend Rupert Frothschild. I shall contact him to ask weather he can send the artefact your way. As for payment, the usual sum shall be apprropriate. All the best,
Laura
i: “I presume you were reffering to their respective busts?”
Referring
A common spelling mistake. The correct answer is referring.
“…I can send that by courrier as soon as possible.”
Courier
A common spelling mistake. The correct answer is courier.
“The bust of Pythagoras is still on lawn to my dear friend…”
Loan
‘Lawn’ does not make sense in the situation and is a look-a-like word to our correct answer, loan.
“I shall contact him to ask weather he can send...”
Whether
‘Weather’ does not make sense in the situation and is a look-a-like word to our correct answer, whether.
“…the usual sum shall be apprropriate.”
Appropriate
This is a spelling error with the word ‘apprropriate’. The correct spelling is ‘appropriate’.

sets.p:
1. That price seems about right.
2. What a bargain! That was better than I expected.
3. Ridiculous offer. Don’t even think about it.
4. Wow, you didn’t do well haggling the price there at all, though I’m not surprised.
5. That’s good, I was hoping it wouldn’t be much more than that.
i: That price seems about right.
3rd
The response is neutral and un-committal. As such, this fits as our middle ranking of 3rd.
What a bargain! That was better than I expected.
1st
This response is very positive, especially in comparation to the other passages that are less so. As such, this fits as our top ranking of 1st.
Ridiculous offer. Don’t even think about it.
4th

This response is not a friendly response and is slightly accusatory. However, it offers some advice and doesn’t place the blame on the person but rather on the offer which makes it a less personal accusation. Therefore, it is not the most negative but ranks 4th.
Wow, you didn’t do well haggling the price there at all, though I’m not surprised.
5th
This is harsh in tone, almost jeering. It places blame on the person rather than the offer. Therefore, this is the most negative and thus is ranked 5th.
That’s good, I was hoping it wouldn’t be much more than that.
2nd
This response is nice and positive though not quite as enthusiastic as the second phrase. Therefore, it is ranked 2nd.

sets.p: Thank you for informing me of your correspondence with Laura. The bust of Parmenides shall be arriving at 10:00 on Friday and will be placed next to the bust of Pythagoras – which is already here at the museum. As you are aware, my lecture will start at 13:00 and conclude one hour later – only then shall we have coffee and take questions. Please give my thanks to Professor Frothschild, and tell our curator, Jane Bennett, that she is due to meet with him 30 minutes after my lecture concludes.
i: The bust of Pythagoras is due to arrive at 10:00 on Friday.
False
False – Line 2 states that the bust of Pythagoras has already arrived at the museum.
Jane Bennett is due to meet Professor Frothschild at 14:30.
True

True – Line 3 states that the lecture will conclude one hour after 13:00 – hence, 14:00. Line 4 states that Jane Bennett is due to meet Professor Frothschild 30 minutes after that – hence, 14:30. Therefore, the statement is true.
The bust of Parmenides will be placed to the right of Pythagoras’ bust.
Cannot Say

Cannot Say – Though line 2 states that the bust of Parmenides will be placed next to the bust of Pythagoras, it does not state one which side it will be placed. Therefore, we have insufficient information and cannot say.
Coffee will be served at 13:30.
False
False – Line 3 states that the lecture will be taking place from 13:00 – 14:00 and that coffee will be served AFTER the end and ONLY after the end. Therefore, coffee will not be served at 13:30.
The director’s lecture will be mainly about Pythagoras.
Cannot Say
Cannot Say – There is no mention in the passage of the lecture subject matter nor how the time will be allocated.
